(ii) In the same way \angle SBT = 90^\circ (using Q). \angle SAT and \angle SBT are both right angles on the interval ST, so A and B lie on the circle with diameter ST (angle in a semicircle, converse).

prompt:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for n≥1,
3−6+12−24+⋯+3(−2)n−1=1−(−2)n.
stmt_text: Prove by mathematical induction that, for n \ge 1,3 - 6 + 12 - 24 + \cdots + 3(-2)^{n-1} = 1 - (-2)^n.
sol_text:
Model answer:
Step 1. n = 1: LHS = 3, RHS = 1 - (-2) = 3. True.
Step 2. Assume true for n = k: 3 - 6 + \cdots + 3(-2)^{k-1} = 1 - (-2)^k.
Step 3. For n = k + 1: LHS = 1 - (-2)^k + 3(-2)^k = 1 + 2(-2)^k = 1 - (-2)(-2)^k = 1 - (-2)^{k+1}, the RHS for n = k + 1.
So if true for n = k it is true for n = k + 1; since true for n = 1, by induction it is true for all n \ge 1.

Step 1. n=1: LHS =3, RHS =1−(−2)=3. True.

Step 2. Assume true for n=k: 3−6+⋯+3(−2)k−1=1−(−2)k.

Step 3. For n=k+1: LHS =1−(−2)k+3(−2)k=1+2(−2)k=1−(−2)(−2)k=1−(−2)k+1, the RHS for n=k+1.

stmt_text: An object is projected from the origin with initial speed V at an angle \theta to the horizontal. Its equations of motion are x = Vt\cos\theta and y = Vt\sin\theta - \dfrac{gt^2}{2} (do NOT prove these).(i) Show that the horizontal range is \dfrac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta. 2(ii) Show that projecting at \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta gives the same horizontal range. 1(iii) The object is projected with speed V to land a horizontal distance d away, where d is less than the maximum range. There are two possible angles, \alpha and \beta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha. [diagram] Let T_\alpha and T_\beta be the times of flight at these two angles. Show that T_\alpha T_\beta = \dfrac{2d}{g}. 3
sol_text:
Model answer:
(i) y = 0 when t\left(V\sin\theta - \frac{gt}{2}\right) = 0, so the time of flight is t = \dfrac{2V\sin\theta}{g}.
Range = V\cos\theta \times \dfrac{2V\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{V^2}{g} \times 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{V^2}{g}\sin 2\theta.

stmt_text: The diagram shows quadrilateral ABCD and the bisectors of its angles at A, B, C and D. The bisectors at A and B meet at P, the bisectors at A and D meet at Q, the bisectors at C and D meet at R, and the bisectors at B and C meet at S. [diagram] Show that PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral.
sol_text:
Model answer:
Let the angles of ABCD be 2\alpha, 2\beta, 2\gamma, 2\delta at A, B, C, D, so 2\alpha + 2\beta + 2\gamma + 2\delta = 360^\circ and \alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 180^\circ.
In triangle ABP: \angle APB = 180^\circ - \alpha - \beta, and \angle QPS = \angle APB (vertically opposite).
In triangle CDR: \angle DRC = 180^\circ - \gamma - \delta, and \angle QRS = \angle DRC (vertically opposite).
\angle QPS + \angle QRS = 360^\circ - (\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta) = 180^\circ. Opposite angles are supplementary, so PQRS is cyclic.

sol_text:
Model answer:
(i) (1 + (1 + x))^n = \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}(1 + x)^k. The coefficient of x^r in (1 + x)^k is \binom{k}{r} (zero when k < r), so the coefficient of x^r is \displaystyle\sum_{k=r}^{n} \binom{n}{k}\binom{k}{r}.
(2 + x)^n = \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{n} \binom{n}{j}2^{n-j}x^j, whose coefficient of x^r is \binom{n}{r}2^{n-r}. The two expressions are the same polynomial, so the coefficients are equal.

From F a line perpendicular to AC meets AB, a new quadrant centred at F is drawn touching AB in the smaller right triangle, and this is repeated forever, as shown. [diagram] (i) Show that triangles ABC and ACD are similar. 1(ii) Show that x = \dfrac{ab}{c}. 1(iii) Show that the total length of all the quadrant arcs is \dfrac{\pi b}{2}. 4(iv) Hence, or otherwise, show that the radii of all the quadrants add up to b. 1
sol_text:
Model answer:
(i) \angle A is common, and \angle BCA = \angle CDA = 90^\circ, so \triangle ABC \sim \triangle ACD (equiangular).
(ii) Matching sides: \dfrac{CD}{BC} = \dfrac{AC}{AB}, so \dfrac{x}{a} = \dfrac{b}{c} and x = \dfrac{ab}{c}.
(iii) The next right triangle (at F) is similar to ABC, with base AF = b - x instead of b. So every length, including the next radius, is multiplied by \dfrac{b - x}{b} = 1 - \dfrac{a}{c} = \dfrac{c - a}{c}.
The arcs are \frac{\pi}{2}x, \frac{\pi}{2}x\left(\frac{c - a}{c}\right), \dots, a geometric series with ratio \frac{c - a}{c}, which is between 0 and 1 (since 0 < a < c).
Limiting sum = \dfrac{\frac{\pi}{2} \times \frac{ab}{c}}{1 - \frac{c - a}{c}} = \dfrac{\pi ab}{2c} \times \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{\pi b}{2}.
(iv) Each arc is \frac{\pi}{2} times its radius, so the radii add up to \frac{\pi b}{2} \div \frac{\pi}{2} = b. (The centres march along AC towards A.)
